The present invention relates to a hydrogen recycling flight system and flight method. The hydrogen recycling flight system includes: a flight fuselage having at least one pair of wings on both sides of a body; a hydrogen gas balloon airtightly connected to the flight fuselage; a hydrogen fuel cell connected to the hydrogen gas balloon and installed outside or inside the flight fuselage; and a secondary battery charged with electricity generated by the hydrogen fuel cell, electricity generated by a solar cell provided on an outer peripheral portion of the flight fuselage, or electricity supplied from an external power network.

By using a switch, the hydrogen fuel cell is switched to function as a water electrolysis device, or the water electrolysis device is switched to function as the hydrogen fuel cell. The hydrogen recycling flight system further includes: a water tank configured to store water generated from the hydrogen fuel cell; the water electrolysis device configured to electrolyze the stored water; a switch control device configured to switch the functions of the hydrogen fuel cell and the water electrolysis device; and a high-pressure gas barrel configured to store, at high pressure, hydrogen gas and oxygen gas generated in the water electrolysis device.

The flight fuselage flies by controlling the volume of the hydrogen gas balloon, which provides flotation power for a flight vehicle, through operation of the hydrogen fuel cell or the high-pressure gas barrel.

The invention concerns a flight system and flight method based on hydrogen recycling. The system comprises a flight fuselage having at least one pair of wings on both lateral sides of its body; a hydrogen gas balloon hermetically coupled to the flight fuselage; a hydrogen fuel cell connected to the hydrogen gas balloon and mounted either inside or outside the fuselage; and a secondary battery that can be charged using power produced by the hydrogen fuel cell, power generated by a solar cell positioned on an outer peripheral part of the fuselage, or electricity supplied from an external power grid.

In this system, a switch enables the hydrogen fuel cell to be changed over to function as a water electrolysis device, or the water electrolysis device to be changed over to function as the hydrogen fuel cell. The hydrogen recycling flight system further includes a water tank for holding water produced by the hydrogen fuel cell; the water electrolysis device for electrolyzing the stored water; a switch control device for changing the functions of the hydrogen fuel cell and the water electrolysis device; and a high-pressure gas cylinder for storing, under high pressure, hydrogen gas and oxygen gas produced by the water electrolysis device.

The flight fuselage is configured to fly by regulating the volume of the hydrogen gas balloon, which provides buoyant force for the flight vehicle, through operation of either the hydrogen fuel cell or the high-pressure gas cylinder.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a hydrogen recycling flight system designed for a flight vehicle having a fuselage and wings. The system includes a hydrogen gas balloon, a hydrogen fuel cell, and a secondary battery, which together provide both lift control and power management during flight.

In this system, the secondary battery serves as an electrical energy storage unit. It may be charged in several ways, including by electricity generated from the hydrogen fuel cell, by solar cells mounted on the fuselage, or by connection to an external power network when the flight vehicle is on the ground. This arrangement allows the vehicle to store energy from multiple sources and use it as needed during operation.

A switch control device is provided to selectively change the operating mode of the system. In one mode, the hydrogen fuel cell consumes hydrogen and oxygen to generate electrical power. In another mode, the system performs water electrolysis, using electrical energy to decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen. By switching between these modes, the flight system can recycle hydrogen and manage its energy resources more efficiently.

During fuel cell operation, the hydrogen fuel cell produces water as a by-product. This water is collected and stored in a water tank. When electrolysis operation is selected, the stored water is electrolyzed to generate hydrogen and oxygen. The generated hydrogen can then be reused in the flight system, while the oxygen may also be stored or supplied to the fuel cell as required.

The flight vehicle further controls buoyancy by adjusting the volume of the hydrogen gas balloon. Hydrogen may be supplied to the balloon from the hydrogen fuel cell system or from a high-pressure gas barrel. By increasing or decreasing the amount of hydrogen in the gas balloon, the vehicle can regulate its lifting force and improve flight stability. This hydrogen recycling arrangement enables efficient use of fuel, supports long-duration flight, and provides a practical mechanism for managing both propulsion energy and buoyancy.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to a sustainable flight vehicle and propulsion system that uses recyclable hydrogen as both an energy source and a buoyancy-control medium. The flight vehicle includes a fuselage, wings, a hydrogen balloon or gas envelope, a hydrogen fuel cell, a secondary battery, a solar charging unit or external charging port, a water storage tank, an electrolysis device, a switch controller, and a high-pressure gas storage unit. These components cooperate to provide propulsion power, electrical energy storage, hydrogen generation, oxygen generation, and controlled flotation during flight.

In one configuration, the fuselage supports the wings and contains the main power and control components. The hydrogen balloon is connected to the fuselage and is capable of being inflated or deflated to adjust the buoyant force acting on the vehicle. The high-pressure gas storage unit stores hydrogen produced by the electrolysis device or supplied from an external source. When hydrogen is supplied to the balloon, the balloon expands and increases lift or flotation. When hydrogen is withdrawn or compressed into storage, the balloon volume is reduced, allowing the vehicle to decrease buoyancy, descend, or adjust its attitude and altitude more efficiently.

The fuel cell receives hydrogen and oxygen and generates electrical power for the propulsion system, control electronics, and other onboard equipment. Electrical power may also be supplied to or stored in the secondary battery. The secondary battery functions as an auxiliary or buffer power source, supplying energy during takeoff, peak power demand, fuel-cell startup, or periods when hydrogen generation is insufficient. The battery may be charged by the fuel cell, by solar panels mounted on the wings or fuselage, or through an external charging device when the aircraft is on the ground.

During operation, water stored in the water tank is supplied to the electrolysis device. The electrolysis device uses electrical energy from the solar charging unit, secondary battery, fuel cell, or an external source to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The generated hydrogen may be directed to the high-pressure gas storage unit, the fuel cell, or the hydrogen balloon. The generated oxygen may be supplied to the fuel cell to support electricity generation or may be stored or released depending on the operating condition. As the fuel cell operates, it combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity and water. The water produced by the fuel cell can be returned to the water tank, thereby forming a recycling loop in which water is repeatedly converted into hydrogen and oxygen and then recombined to produce power.

The switch controller controls the flow of electrical energy and gases among the fuel cell, battery, solar charging unit, electrolysis device, water tank, hydrogen balloon, and high-pressure storage unit. The controller may select an operating mode according to flight conditions, remaining battery charge, hydrogen pressure, balloon volume, altitude, propulsion demand, and available solar energy. For example, during ascent, the controller may supply hydrogen to the balloon to increase buoyancy and reduce the propulsion energy required for climbing. During level flight, the controller may operate the fuel cell and battery together to maintain efficient propulsion. During descent or landing, the controller may reduce the balloon volume by transferring hydrogen from the balloon to the high-pressure storage unit, thereby decreasing lift and improving altitude control.

The invention therefore provides a flight system capable of extending flight duration by reusing onboard water and hydrogen resources. By combining fuel-cell power generation, electrolysis, rechargeable battery storage, solar or external charging, and variable-volume hydrogen buoyancy control, the vehicle can reduce energy consumption compared with conventional aircraft that rely only on engine thrust for lift and propulsion. The hydrogen balloon provides flotation assistance, while the wings provide aerodynamic lift during forward movement. This hybrid lift arrangement allows the propulsion system to operate at lower power for longer periods.

A principal advantage of the invention is that hydrogen is not merely consumed and discarded, but is managed as part of a recyclable energy cycle. Water generated by the fuel cell is collected and reused, while hydrogen generated by electrolysis can be stored, used for fuel-cell operation, or supplied to the buoyancy balloon. The system also improves flight efficiency by allowing buoyancy to be adjusted according to mission requirements. As a result, the invention enables a reusable hydrogen-based flight vehicle with longer endurance, reduced fuel waste, improved energy efficiency, and enhanced control over flotation and altitude.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. As a definite article, “the” helps identify a specific person, place, thing, or idea. For example, saying “the book” tells the listener that we are talking about a particular book, not just any book.

Although it may seem simple, “the” gives sentences clarity and precision. It guides the reader or listener toward something known, shared, or already mentioned. In phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” or “the future,” the word adds focus and meaning.

“The” is a reminder that even the smallest words can have great importance. Without it, English would sound less natural and less exact. This tiny word helps connect ideas, create understanding, and make language more effective.

counterfactuals.output: A hydrogen recycling flight system includes a hydrogen balloon configured to generate lift, a fuel cell configured to consume hydrogen and oxygen to produce electric power and water, a solar charging unit configured to supply renewable electrical energy, an electrolyzer configured to electrolyze water into hydrogen and oxygen, a secondary battery configured to store electrical energy, a water tank configured to store water produced by the fuel cell and supplied to the electrolyzer, a high-pressure gas storage unit configured to store compressed hydrogen, and a switch controller configured to selectively control power flow, gas flow, and operating modes of the system. During flight, hydrogen may be supplied from the balloon or the high-pressure gas storage unit to the fuel cell to generate electricity for propulsion, avionics, and auxiliary loads, while produced water is collected in the water tank. When solar power or stored battery power is available, the electrolyzer converts the stored water into hydrogen for replenishing the balloon or the high-pressure gas storage unit. The switch controller regulates hydrogen generation, compression, storage, fuel-cell operation, battery charging, and gas transfer to adjust buoyancy, maintain flight altitude, and recycle hydrogen and water within the system, thereby enabling extended-duration flight with reduced fuel loss and improved energy efficiency.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description in the format of a patent claim for an airship-like flight vehicle that recycles hydrogen by converting fuel-cell water back into hydrogen and oxygen through electrolysis.
counterfactuals.output:
1. **An airship-type flight vehicle**, comprising:  
   a buoyant hull defining at least one internal lift-gas chamber configured to contain hydrogen as a lifting gas;  
   a propulsion system configured to generate thrust for controlled flight of the vehicle;  
   a fuel-cell power system fluidly coupled to a hydrogen supply and an oxygen-containing oxidant supply, the fuel-cell power system being configured to electrochemically generate electrical power and produce water as a reaction product;  
   a water recovery system configured to collect at least a portion of the water produced by the fuel-cell power system;  
   an electrolyzer fluidly coupled to the water recovery system and configured to electrolyze the collected water into regenerated hydrogen and oxygen; and  
   a gas management system configured to direct at least a portion of the regenerated hydrogen to the at least one lift-gas chamber, to the hydrogen supply of the fuel-cell power system, or to both, thereby recycling hydrogen consumed by the fuel-cell power system during operation of the flight vehicle.

2. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the gas management system comprises one or more compressors, pumps, valves, regulators, manifolds, or flow controllers configured to selectively transfer regenerated hydrogen between the electrolyzer, a hydrogen storage vessel, the fuel-cell power system, and the at least one lift-gas chamber.

3. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, further comprising an electrical energy source coupled to the electrolyzer, the electrical energy source comprising one or more of photovoltaic panels, a battery, a supercapacitor, a wind-driven generator, or excess electrical output from the fuel-cell power system.

4. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 3**, wherein the electrolyzer is operated when available electrical power exceeds propulsion or avionics demand, thereby converting surplus electrical energy into stored chemical energy in the form of regenerated hydrogen.

5. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the oxygen generated by the electrolyzer is vented overboard, stored in an oxygen storage vessel, supplied to the fuel-cell power system, or supplied to an environmental control system.

6. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the water recovery system comprises a condenser configured to condense water vapor from an exhaust stream of the fuel-cell power system.

7. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, further comprising a control system configured to monitor one or more of hydrogen pressure, hydrogen purity, oxygen concentration, water inventory, electrical demand, buoyancy, altitude, and lift-gas chamber pressure, and to control operation of the electrolyzer and gas management system in response thereto.

8. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 7**, wherein the control system is configured to maintain a buoyancy setpoint by regulating delivery of regenerated hydrogen to the at least one lift-gas chamber.

9. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the at least one lift-gas chamber comprises a plurality of independently controllable hydrogen cells, and wherein the gas management system is configured to distribute regenerated hydrogen among the plurality of hydrogen cells to control trim, buoyancy, or center of lift.

10. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, further comprising a hydrogen purification device positioned downstream of the electrolyzer and configured to remove water vapor, oxygen, or contaminants from the regenerated hydrogen before delivery to the at least one lift-gas chamber or the fuel-cell power system.

11. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the fuel-cell power system comprises a proton-exchange membrane fuel cell, and the electrolyzer comprises a proton-exchange membrane electrolyzer.

12. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, wherein the propulsion system comprises one or more electrically driven propulsors powered at least in part by the fuel-cell power system.

13. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, further comprising a hydrogen buffer storage tank fluidly connected between the electrolyzer and the fuel-cell power system to accommodate differences between a rate of hydrogen generation by the electrolyzer and a rate of hydrogen consumption by the fuel-cell power system.

14. **The airship-type flight vehicle of claim 1**, further comprising a safety system including at least one hydrogen sensor and at least one vent or isolation valve configured to mitigate accumulation of hydrogen outside the at least one lift-gas chamber.

15. **A method of operating an airship-type flight vehicle**, comprising:  
   supplying hydrogen to a fuel-cell power system onboard the flight vehicle;  
   generating electrical power in the fuel-cell power system to power at least one onboard load, the fuel-cell power system producing water;  
   collecting at least a portion of the water produced by the fuel-cell power system;  
   electrolyzing the collected water onboard the flight vehicle to produce regenerated hydrogen and oxygen; and  
   directing at least a portion of the regenerated hydrogen to a hydrogen lift-gas chamber, to the fuel-cell power system, or to both, thereby recycling hydrogen during flight.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an invention summary for a hydrogen-powered flying fuselage with wings, a hydrogen gas balloon, hydrogen fuel cell/electrolyzer switching device, battery, solar cell, water tank, and high-pressure gas barrel.
counterfactuals.output:
## Invention Summary

The invention relates to a hydrogen-powered flying fuselage aircraft that combines lighter-than-air lift, aerodynamic lift, electric propulsion, solar energy collection, hydrogen energy storage, and onboard hydrogen regeneration. The aircraft includes a fuselage provided with wings, a hydrogen gas balloon, an electric propulsion system, a hydrogen fuel cell/electrolyzer switching device, a battery, solar cells, a water tank, and a high-pressure hydrogen gas barrel.

In operation, the hydrogen gas balloon provides buoyant lift to reduce the effective weight of the aircraft, while the wings generate aerodynamic lift during forward motion. Electric motors powered by the battery and/or hydrogen fuel cell drive propellers or other thrust devices to propel the aircraft. The hydrogen fuel cell consumes hydrogen from the high-pressure gas barrel and oxygen from ambient air to generate electricity, with water produced as a byproduct. The produced water may be collected in the water tank.

The solar cells are mounted on the fuselage, wings, or balloon surface and generate electrical power during daylight. This power may be supplied directly to the aircraft electrical system, stored in the battery, or used by the fuel cell/electrolyzer switching device in an electrolyzer mode. In electrolyzer mode, water from the water tank is decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen. The generated hydrogen may be stored in the high-pressure gas barrel and/or supplied to the hydrogen balloon, thereby extending flight endurance and improving energy self-sufficiency.

The hydrogen fuel cell/electrolyzer switching device selectively operates either as a fuel cell to produce electricity from hydrogen or as an electrolyzer to produce hydrogen from water using electrical energy from the solar cells or battery. The battery functions as an energy buffer, supplying peak power during takeoff, climb, maneuvering, or low solar output, and receiving charge from the solar cells or fuel cell when excess power is available.

The high-pressure gas barrel stores compressed hydrogen for propulsion energy and for replenishing the hydrogen balloon as needed. The water tank stores water for electrolysis and may also collect water generated by the fuel cell. A control system may manage switching between fuel-cell mode, electrolysis mode, battery charging, hydrogen storage, balloon replenishment, and propulsion power delivery according to flight conditions, energy demand, solar availability, hydrogen pressure, and battery state of charge.

This configuration enables an aircraft with reduced energy consumption due to combined buoyant and aerodynamic lift, extended range through hydrogen fuel-cell power, renewable energy input from solar cells, and partial closed-loop reuse of water and hydrogen. The invention is suitable for long-endurance flight, unmanned aerial vehicles, environmental monitoring, communications relay, cargo transport, and low-emission aviation applications.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a patent abstract for a flight system where a hydrogen fuel cell can be switched into a water electrolysis device, stores generated gases under pressure, and adjusts the volume of a hydrogen balloon to fly.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

A flight system includes a buoyant envelope containing a variable volume of hydrogen gas, a reversible electrochemical unit selectively operable in a fuel-cell mode and an electrolysis mode, pressurized gas storage vessels, and a control system. In the fuel-cell mode, hydrogen and oxygen are supplied to the electrochemical unit to generate electrical power and water. In the electrolysis mode, electrical power is supplied to the electrochemical unit to separate water into hydrogen and oxygen, which are compressed or otherwise stored in respective pressurized storage vessels. The control system regulates transfer of hydrogen between the storage vessel and the buoyant envelope to increase or decrease the envelope volume and thereby control lift, altitude, or descent of the aircraft. Oxygen may be stored for later fuel-cell operation or vented. The system enables repeated conversion between stored chemical energy, electrical energy, water, and buoyant hydrogen gas to provide propulsion, onboard power, and controlled aerostatic flight.
